analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to give rebates for drugs used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: A bill to make drug makers pay rebates on medicines used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries was introduced in June 2011, referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Henry Waxman introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act of 2011 on June 15, 2011. The bill would require drug manufacturers to sign rebate agreements with the Secretary of Health and Human Services and pay the government rebates on prescription drugs used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries. If a manufacturer refused to sign a rebate agreement, its drugs could no longer be covered under Medicare's Part D drug benefit. The bill also required private Medicare drug plans to report price concessions and rebates, with civil money penalties for failures. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then to their Health subcommittees on June 22 and 23, 2011. No committee action, no floor vote, and no vote ever followed; the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still sitting in subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicare beneficiaries, such as people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid or receive low-income drug subsidies, would pay less out of pocket for prescriptions under the bill. The federal government would also save money, because a large share of the cost of low-income beneficiaries' drugs is taxpayer-funded through the low-income and reinsurance subsidies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires drug manufacturers to pay the Secretary of Health and Human Services rebates on drugs used by Medicare beneficiaries covered under the Part D prescription drug benefit, mirroring the rebates manufacturers already owe under Medicaid.

It excludes from Medicare Part D coverage any drug made by a manufacturer that has not entered into and has in effect a rebate agreement with the Secretary, giving manufacturers a strong incentive to pay the rebates.

It requires private Medicare drug plans (PDP sponsors) to report price concessions and rebates for their drugs to the Secretary, and provides for civil money penalties on top of other penalties, aimed at making sure taxpayers do not overpay on drugs covered by low-income and reinsurance subsidies.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, who would owe new rebates on drugs used by rebate-eligible Medicare beneficiaries. The Congressional Budget Office traditionally scores such Medicaid-style rebate extensions for Medicare as large federal savings, which come directly out of manufacturer revenue on those drugs. Some of that cost could be offset through higher list prices on other drugs, a trade-off critics of rebate mandates have long pointed to.

drawbacks.text: The rebates apply only to a defined group of "rebate eligible" Medicare beneficiaries, not to Medicare beneficiaries generally, so most seniors' drug costs would be unchanged by the bill.

Mandated manufacturer rebates are a cost to drug companies, and industry opponents have long argued such mandates discourage investment in new medicines and can push list prices up for drugs outside the rebate program; the bill's exclusion of non-participating manufacturers' drugs from Part D coverage would also restrict formulary choices for plans.
The bill places new reporting duties and civil money penalty exposure on private Medicare drug plan sponsors, which plan insurers would bear as a compliance cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For low-income Medicare beneficiaries and federal taxpayers, the benefits are straightforward: rebates on drugs whose cost is largely government-funded. The costs fall on drug manufacturers, which is why such bills face industry opposition, though opponents argue some of the cost may reappear as higher prices on drugs not covered by the rebate requirement. The bill never received a hearing or vote, so it was never publicly scored or weighed on its merits in either committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, no action was ever taken, and it died there when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Henry Waxman (D-CA) introduced the Medicare Drug Savings Act of 2011 in the House on June 15, 2011.
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; all listed cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republicans signed on.

The bill was referred on June 15, 2011 to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee, each for consideration of the provisions that fell under its jurisdiction.
On June 22 and June 23, 2011, the bill was referred to the health subcommittees of those committees.

No committee markup, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed. The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill still pending in subcommittee, so it never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they never had to pay the new rebates on drugs used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries, and Medicare Part D plans were spared new reporting requirements and penalty exposure. Low-income Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers continue to pay the full negotiated prices for those drugs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers, which avoided paying rebates

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman (D-CA)
for.role: Sponsor, senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2011 and designated it for referral to Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.

for.name: 14 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 14 were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means subcommittee leadership
against.role: The committees and health subcommittees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its June 2011 referral to the Health subcommittees; it was never marked up, reported, or scheduled for a floor vote during the 112th Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: The industry that would have owed the new Medicare rebates
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending Medicaid-style rebates to Medicare during this period, as the industry has publicly done for similar proposals.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken in committee or on the floor. Support was one-sided on paper: the sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-held committees never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would require manufacturers to pay the government rebates on drugs used by low-income Medicare beneficiaries and would strip Part D coverage from the drugs of any manufacturer that refused a rebate agreement. That is a direct revenue loss, and the industry's interest in blocking the bill runs against beneficiaries and taxpayers who would otherwise pay full price.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors (private insurers and PBMs)
industries.note: The bill would impose new duties on Part D plans to report price concessions and rebates to the Secretary, with civil money penalties for failures, while leaving their role as the channel through which Medicare's low-income drug subsidies flow intact.
